5.text: Late in the fall, or rather in the beginning of the winter, the chief cere-

6.text: monial of the year is performed. It is consecrated to Kereˊtkun, or is made

7.text: a thanksgiving ceremonial to the spirits of sea-mammals killed since the fall.

8.text: Early in spring there follows the ceremonial of boats, which are made ready

9.text: for the approaching season. In the middle of summer the ceremonial of

10.text: “heads” is performed. This is for thanksgiving to the spirits of sea-mammals

11.text: killed since early in the spring.

12.text: These four ceremonials are performed with varying similarity by both

16.text: Most of the Maritime Chukchee offer sacrifice also in midwinter to the

17.text: star Pehiˊttin,¹ and perform in the middle of spring a ceremonial analogous

18.text: to the ceremonial of antlers of the reindeer-breeders, which is called by the

19.text: same name, Kiˊlvei. The sacrifice to the whale is performed, in addition,

20.text: each time after a whale has been killed or has drifted ashore.

21.text: Bloody and bloodless sacrifices are offered during these ceremonials.

22.text: The Maritime Chukchee of course can slaughter only dogs for their bloody

23.text: sacrifices. In comparison with the Koryak, however, they are merciful to

24.text: their dogs, and kill them in no very great numbers. In this, as in other

25.text: respects, they occupy a middle ground between the American Eskimo, who

26.text: do not sacrifice dogs, and the Koryak, who often kill almost all the animals

28.text: Ceremonial House. — According to information given by the natives,

29.text: and also by inference from the example of Nuˊnlig̣ren, most of the villages

30.text: have each a special house intended for the performance of the chief ceremonial

31.text: of the winter. This house, however, differs in many respects from the kaˊshim

32.text: of the American Eskimo. Its size is that of the houses ordinarily in use;

33.text: and often it is really a house left by its owner, for some particular reasons,

34.text: for another dwelling. In many instances it was the private property of a
